The Melon butterflyfish Chaetodon trifasciatus exhibits a life-history strategy typical of many coral reef-associated chaetodontids, with a maximum recorded adult body mass of 93 grams [Wwi = 93 grams] attained at an asymptotic length. Field surveys across the Indo-Pacific indicate that individuals rarely exceed an ultimate total length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a size constraint linked to the structural complexity of branching coral substrates they inhabit. Under stable thermal conditions characteristic of shallow reef flats at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the incubation period from gamete fusion to hatching is relatively brief, with the embryo undergoing cleavage and subsequent organogenesis inside a transparent, yolk-laden egg. The age at birth, defined as the moment of chorion rupture and larval eclosion, is approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], a duration consistent with the rapid developmental rates observed in other small-bodied butterflyfishes. Upon emergence, the prolarva remains entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, initiating exogenous feeding only after the yolk-sac is fully resorbed, a critical transition that determines early survival.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds gradually, with individuals attaining puberty at a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], a size that corresponds to roughly half the ultimate body length. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 9 grams [Wwp = approximately 9 grams], a modest mass that nonetheless appears sufficient to support the energetic demands of gonad maturation and gametogenesis, consistent with the relatively low fecundity per spawning event observed in this genus. Histological examination of gonadal tissue shows that vitellogenesis begins after this size threshold, and the gonadosomatic index (GSI) peaked at approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] during the spawning season at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. The protracted reproductive window likely buffers against stochastic variations in prey availability and coral cover.

The modest egg diameter of approximately 0.75 millimeters, inferred from closely related butterflyfishes, yields newly hatched larvae with a wet weight at birth of only 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], placing this species at the extreme lower end of larval size among coral reef teleosts. This minute initial mass imposes a severe energetic constraint during the yolk-sac larva stage, as the lecithotrophic larva must absorb its limited endogenous nutrients before the onset of first exogenous feeding. Mortality rates during this pelagic larval phase are consequently high, with survival heavily dependent on rapid yolk absorption and successful prey capture once the mouth opens and the swim bladder inflates. The transition from endotrophy to exotrophy represents a major bottleneck in the early life history, and any delay in first feeding can lead to the point of no return, after which larvae cannot recover despite adequate prey availability. Morphological differentiation during this period includes retinal maturation, enabling prey detection, and the gradual ossification of fin rays.

Longevity estimates for Chaetodon trifasciatus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] when maintained at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], a remarkably extended duration for a teleost of its modest body size. This longevity is broadly consistent with the slow life-history pace observed across the genus, likely reflecting the stable, low-mortality environment of coral reef ecosystems where predation risk is moderate and food resources, primarily coral polyps and small benthic invertebrates, are predictably available. The old age attained by some individuals suggests that reproductive senescence may occur late in life, with gravid females still contributing to recruitment well beyond their peak reproductive years. Post-settlement juveniles, which undergo a pronounced habitat transition from a pelagic existence to a benthic, reef-associated lifestyle, benefit from the extended parental investment inherent in iteroparous spawning, as repeated reproductive bouts enhance the probability of offspring encountering favorable settlement conditions following larval metamorphosis.

The species attains a maximum body length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], which is typical for chaetodontids of intermediate body size, and corresponding adult body mass of 93 grams [Wwi = 93 grams] align closely with predictions from length-mass allometries derived for the genus, specifically the relationship using the coefficient 0.02344 and exponent 3.06. Field studies further indicate that the wet weight at puberty of approximately 9 grams [Wwp = approximately 9 grams] is reached by approximately half of the cohort by the end of their second year, though individual variation in growth rates, driven by local food availability and competitive interactions, can shift this timeline by several months. The embryonic period of 7 days [ab = 7 days] at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] remains invariant across populations, underscoring the strong thermal dependence of developmental rates in this ectothermic lineage.
